lesson.title: The One Point Where Every Equation Tells the Truth
lesson.summary: A solution of a system is an ordered pair that satisfies every equation in the system at the same time, not just one of them, and it corresponds to the point where the equations' graphs meet.
lesson.body:
When you solve one linear equation in two variables, like x + y = 5, you get infinitely many ordered pairs that work: (0, 5), (1, 4), (2, 3), and so on, because a single equation only places one restriction on the relationship between x and y. A system of equations asks for something much stronger. It gives you two or more equations at once and asks for the ordered pair, or pairs, that make every equation in the list true simultaneously. That extra requirement is what turns an infinite family of answers into, usually, just one, since each additional equation adds one more restriction that the previous answers must also satisfy.

Since each linear equation in two variables graphs as a straight line, a solution of the system corresponds to a point that lies on every one of those lines at the same time. For a system of two equations, that means the solution is the point where the two lines cross. Any point that sits on only one of the lines fails the system, even though it happens to satisfy one of the equations perfectly. This geometric picture is why the word system is used at all: the equations are meant to be considered as a package, and a true solution has to hold the whole package together, not just one piece of it.

Consider the system 2x + y = 7 and x - y = 2. Adding the two equations eliminates y, since +y and -y cancel: (2x + y) + (x - y) = 7 + 2, which simplifies to 3x = 9, so x = 3. Substituting x = 3 into the second equation gives 3 - y = 2, so y = 1. The candidate solution is the ordered pair (3, 1). To confirm it is genuinely a solution of the system, and not just of one equation, plug it into both originals: 2(3) + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7, which matches the first equation, and 3 - 1 = 2, which matches the second. Because both statements come out true, (3, 1) is confirmed as the solution of the system, and it is the one and only point where the lines 2x + y = 7 and x - y = 2 cross on the coordinate plane.

This checking step matters more than it might seem. A pair like (5, -3) satisfies 2x + y = 7, since 2(5) + (-3) = 10 - 3 = 7, but unless it also satisfies x - y = 2, it is not a solution of the system, only of one equation in it. Since 5 - (-3) = 8, not 2, that pair fails, and it should be rejected as a solution of the system even though half the check passed. Whenever you are handed a candidate answer, whether from a classmate, a graph read by eye, or your own algebra, the only reliable check is substituting into every equation in the system and confirming that each one becomes a true numerical statement, with no exceptions allowed.

Not every system behaves as neatly as this one. Later sections examine what happens when a system's lines never cross at all, giving no solution, or when the two equations secretly describe the same line, giving infinitely many solutions. Recognizing what a solution actually means, an ordered pair that satisfies every equation at once, is the foundation for sorting systems into those categories and for trusting the answers that the graphing, substitution, and elimination methods produce, no matter which of those methods is used to find the candidate pair in the first place.
